messages.subject: Influence of fixed effect prior for multiple intercepts
messages.subject_clean: Influence of fixed effect prior for multiple intercepts
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am working with a two likelihood model such as :
y1 ~ intercept + int1 + covariates
y1 ~ intercept + int2 + covariates
Both likelihoods are gaussian, the only difference between the two dataset is the non-null int1 and int2 (it represents the non-null systematic random error in two different datasets).
The latent field z ~ intercept + covariates

Doing so, I have an idea of priors I would like to set on int1, int2 and intercept to help the model:
int1 ~ N(a=0.5, sigma2=0.5)    #data1 has a mean error around 0.5
int2 ~ N(b=1.5, sigma2=1)       #data2 has a mean error around 0.5
intercept ~N(25, sigma=0.1)     # this is the common intercept between data1 and data2

Here is my call to inla:
inla(Y ~ -1 + int1 + int2 + intercept + covariates,
  data = list(Y = Y, int1 = int1, int2 = int2, intercept= intercept, covariates=covariates),
  family = c("gaussian", "gaussian"),
  control.fixed = list(mean=list(int1=0.5, int2=1.5, intercept=25, default=0),
prec=list(int1=2, int2=1, int.joint=10, default=0.001)))

My problem: intercept posterior marginals (I look at model summary means) are so far from my prior mean. I would intuitively say that if I increase prec, my prior mean will more influence the model but I must be mistaken because it does not evolve like that.

I created another very simple toy example to see the influence of prior on intercept marginal posterior and outputs are counterintuitive to me (it seems like prior on the mean does not change anything):

# -------------------
#  toy example
# -------------------

n=1000
y <- rnorm(n, mean=22, sd=0.01) + rnorm(n, mean=0.5, sd=0.2)

# two different intercepts
int1 <- c(rep(1, n))
int2 <- c(rep(1, n))

# prec on car
mod1 <- inla(Y ~ -1 + int1 + int2,
  data = list(Y = y, int1 = int1, int2= int2),
  family = c("gaussian"),
  control.fixed = list(mean=list(int1=0.5, int2=22), prec=list(int1=1)))

summary(mod1)

# prec on temp.reg
mod2 <- inla(Y ~ -1 + int1 + int2,
  data = list(Y = y, int1 = int1, int2= int2),
  family = c("gaussian"),
  control.fixed = list(mean=list(int1=0.5, int2=22), prec=list(int2=1)))

summary(mod2)

Maybe this example is absurd but I would appreciate some help to find out more about the influence of priors on marginal posterior for fixed effects (I am sure that I do not understand everything...)

Thank you very much !
Eva

messages.subject: Extracting fitted values for the original data only using "inlabru"
messages.subject_clean: Extracting fitted values for the original data only using "inlabru"
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA Team,

I was fitting a spatial coregionalization model using R-INLA, and to extract the fitted values for the original data only, I had made a stack object for prediction and using the following code:

#Stack object for the prediction
stack.pred.jan2022 <-inla.stack(
  data = list(y=cbind(NA,rep(NA, length(jan2022$TM_NP)))),
  A = list(A.pred.jan2022,A.pred.jan2022,1),
  effects = list(list(u.field=1:spde.obs.jan2022$n.spde),
                 list(x.field=1:spde.obs.jan2022$n.spde),
                 data.frame(intercept = rep(1, 50))),
   tag = 'pred')

#The full stack object
stack.full.jan2022 <- inla.stack(stack.x.jan2022, stack.y.jan2022, stack.pred.jan2022)

#Extract the fitted values of the original data only
i.jan2022 <- inla.stack.index(stack.full.jan2022, tag='pred')$data

Now, I am using inlabru instead of inla to allow for SVC model and I am searching for an equivalent method for the above code in order  to extract the fitted values for the original data only to compare the adequacy between the two models

So my question is: How to extract the fitted values for the original data only using "inlabru"?

messages.subject: Logistic model accounting for misclassification ?
messages.subject_clean: Logistic model accounting for misclassification ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA developers,

I am looking at whether it is possible to fit a logistic model accounting for misclassification in R-INLA. One possible specification of such a model could be:

One could also assume a Dirichlet prior for (specificity,sensitivity) to ease the fit (see page 3, https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.408.5656&rep=rep1&type=pdf). Or adding another level and setting sensitivity = 1/(1+exp(-x)), x~ N(e,f) and specificity = 1/(1+exp(-x)), x~ N(g,h).

Given my understanding of the theoretical basement of R-INLA the model in the picture above is probably not included in the LGM class (?) but maybe some kind of trick could be applied so that R-INLA could be used ?

In the same vein, negative binomial/poisson model accounting for misreporting might be a nice addition to the package (e.g.  see https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8950980/), if this kind of model can be implemented.

Best,
Olivier

Additional reference/discussion about binary model with misclassification include:
http://www.jstor.org/stable/2673589
Also discussed here: https://discourse.mc-stan.org/t/logistic-regression-without-a-gold-standard-error-in-observed-classification/28644

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Logistic model accounting for misclassification ?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Logistic model accounting for misclassification ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

this type of model has some aspects in common with partially observed Poisson process models, that lead to slightly nonlinear predictors.  These cannot be done in plain INLA but can be attempted in the inlabru package that adds non-linear predictor support on top of inla.  See for example https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/web/2d_lgcp_distancesampling.html for how those models are implemented.
In your case, you could try writing your predictor as

qlogis( plogis(predictor) * sensitivity_fun(sens_latent) + plogis(predictor, lower.tail = FALSE) * specificity_fun(spec_latent) )

where "predictor" is your ordinary linear predictor expression, and with additional component specifications
  ~ ... + sens(1) + spec(1)

and
sensitivity_fun <- function(x) {
  bru_forward_transformation(qbeta, x, shape1 = ?, shape2 = ?)
}
and similarly for specficity_fun().

If you try it out and have more questions about the inlabru approach, please post on the inlabru github Discussions page, as this would be a hitherto unattempted use case...
We've tried similar models, and one thing to look out for is whether the model is identifiable & unimodal.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I want to fit a binomial model for the following formula, where I group over months over a 10 year period:

Rain_no_days ~ -1 + Intercept + Latitude.cent + Elevation + f(field,
    model = spde.nonstat, group = field.group, control.group = list(model = "ar1"))

result4_binom_early<-inla(formula4_min,  family="binomial", Ntrials=temp_early$Days_per_month,
                          data=inla.stack.data(stack_early, spde=spde.nonstat),
                          control.predictor = list(A=inla.stack.A(stack_early), compute=TRUE,link=1),
                          control.compute = list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE, waic=TRUE, config=TRUE, return.marginals.predictor=TRUE),
                          verbose=TRUE)

Now I want to do prediction. I implement my prediction stack for which I set Rain_no_days to NA but what do I do with the Ntrials? If I leave it with Ntrials=temp_early$Days_per_month I get the following error "  arguments imply differing number of rows: 17378784, 28704".

thanks in advance.

All the best,
Corinna

I am currently trying to follow a tutorial by Elias T Krainski (https://eliaskrainski.github.io/INLAspacetime/vignettes/barrierExample.html).

Thanks for any help!
Andrew Houldcroft

messages.body_plain:
I'm in the process of updating all the spatial-handling code in INLA,
and as part of that I added an fm_contains() method yesterday to
inlabru (replacing inla.over_sp_mesh that only handled some meshes and
sp objects; fm_contains handles both sp and sf polygons, as well as
spherical and globe meshes).

The output of
  unlist(fm_contains(polygon, mesh))
corresponds to the contents of the triBarrier variable in the vignette.

fm_contains currently requires the polygon to be provided as either an
sf object with one or more polygons, or a SpatialPolygons object but
that might be expanded to "raw polygon data" (like in the vignette).
For most spatial problems the barriers are already given as sf or sp objects.

PS. Elias, I think I'll add a method for returning the triangle
centroids since the new code does that internally for all meshes, not
just flat ones, but in the meantime, the vignette code

triCenters <-
    cbind(
        mesh$loc[mesh$graph$tv[,1], 1] +
        mesh$loc[mesh$graph$tv[,2], 1] +
        mesh$loc[mesh$graph$tv[,3], 1],
        mesh$loc[mesh$graph$tv[,1], 2] +
        mesh$loc[mesh$graph$tv[,2], 2] +
        mesh$loc[mesh$graph$tv[,3], 2])/3

can be simplified:

triCenters <-
        (mesh$loc[mesh$graph$tv[,1], ] +
        mesh$loc[mesh$graph$tv[,2], ] +
        mesh$loc[mesh$graph$tv[,3], ]) / 3

Use triCenters[, 1:2] to ignore the third column of the mesh locations.

Finn

messages.subject: Graphing a non-separable model
messages.subject_clean: Graphing a non-separable model
messages.body_plain:
I'm at a point where I need to graph my results from fitting a non-separable inla model to my wind speed data. For the fitting and graphing I use the example given by Haakon Bakka at https://haakonbakkagit.github.io/btopic133.html . The problem I have is with graphing the random effect of my model: Instead of seeing one graph per time period, it seems that the graph shows t.mx <http://t.mx> patterns on one graph - I'm attaching the visual of the estimate and also the true process. The estimate seems to be good, however the graphing part seem to be the problem. I'm including my code hoping that somebody can identify why mistake and I could get some feedback on it. I'm looking at estimating daily wind speeds from a computer model simulations over the course of 6 days.
Thank you for your help!
Eva

Code:

library(fields)
library(maps)

library(viridisLite)
library(gtools)
library(mapdata)
load("Wind_SC.RData")
#load("Wind_smaller.RData")
#Extract one year worth of data for the first 6 days
loc = cbind(c(lonSE_SC), c(latSE_SC))
#loc = cbind(c(lonSE_smaller), c(latSE_smaller))

## Number of time points used
## Subsets the data
t.max = 6

ws = c(r22.SC[,,1:t.max,1])
ws.df <- data.frame(lon = rep(loc[,1], each = t.max),
                    lat = rep(loc[,2], each = t.max),
                    ws= ws,
                    time = rep(1:t.max,  nrow(loc)) )

plot(ws.df$lon, ws.df$lat, col="blue",
     xlab="longitude", ylab="latitude", main="Observation locations")
maps::map("state", add=TRUE, col = grey(.85))
#plot the response change in time
plot(ws.df$time,ws.df$ws )

## Max edge in spatial mesh
## Small number makes algorithm very slow
## ex: 2, 1.5
max.e = 2

## Prior model information
M = list()
for (i in 1:2) M[[i]] = list()
## Posteriors
fits = list()
## stacks (see later)
stack = list()

# Create temporal mesh
mesh.t = inla.mesh.1d(1:t.max)
bnd= inla.nonconvex.hull((cbind(ws.df$lon, ws.df$lat)))
mesh.s2 = inla.mesh.2d(loc = cbind(ws.df$lon, ws.df$lat), boundary = bnd,
                       max.edge = c(0.5,1),
                       cutoff = .3)
plot(mesh.s2);axis(1);axis(2)
points(ws.df$lon, ws.df$lat, pch = 16, col=adjustcolor("black", alpha.f = 0.5))
maps::map("state", add=TRUE, col = grey(.5))
mesh.s2$n*mesh.t$n
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/haakonbakkagit/haakonbakkagit.github.io/master/functions-rgeneric-121-march2020.R", destfile="functions-rgeneric-121-march2020.R")
source("functions-rgeneric-121-march2020.R")
## Model component in space
mco.space <http://mco.space/> = inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh.s2,
                                prior.range = c(600, .6), prior.sigma = c(18, 0.01))

## Mesh in space and time
## Lambdas for exponential prior on transformed hyper-param (1/rt, 1/rs and sig)
rgen.obj = list(mesh.space <http://mesh.space/> = mesh.s2,
                mesh.time = mesh.t,
                lambdas = c(1,1,5))
## Nonsep model definition
nm = mesh.s2$n*mesh.t$n

## The non-separable random effect / random field
mco.nonsep = inla.rgeneric.define(
  model = stmodel121.interpret, debug = FALSE, n = nm, obj = rgen.obj)

i.nonsep = 1:(mesh.s2$n * mesh.t$n)
A.st = inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh.s2, loc = cbind(ws.df$lon, ws.df$lat), group = ws.df$time, group.mesh =mesh.t)

stack[[2]] = inla.stack(
  data = list(y = ws.df$ws),
  effects = list(i.nonsep = i.nonsep),
  A = list(A.st),
  tag = 'stdata')

mco.nonsep.fix = inla.rgeneric.define(model = stmodel121.interpret,
                                      debug = FALSE, n = nm, obj = rgen.obj)
## The formula
## It is possible to add a spatial random effect (uncomment the f(s))
form.nonsep = y ~ -1 + f(i.nonsep, model = mco.nonsep.fix, n = nm)

M[[2]]$formula = form.nonsep

fits[[2]] = inla(M[[2]]$formula,
                 family = "gaussian",
                 data =inla.stack.data(stack[[2]]),
                 control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, A=inla.stack.A(stack[[2]])))

#Plot

time.k = 2
rf.st.nonsep = fits[[2]]$summary.random$i$mean
field.nonsep =rf.st.nonsep[1:mesh.s2$n + (time.k-1)*mesh.s2$n]
zlim.temp = range(field.nonsep)
xlim = c(min(lonSE_SC), max(lonSE_SC)); ylim = c(min(latSE_SC), max(latSE_SC))
proj = inla.mesh.projector(mesh.s2, xlim = xlim,
                             ylim = ylim, dims=c(300, 300))
field.nonsep.proj = inla.mesh.project(proj, field.nonsep)

image.plot(list(x = proj$x, y=proj$y, z = field.nonsep.proj), col = tim.colors(256),
             xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim, zlim = c(0, 16))
title("Estimated process using a separable covariance")
#points(ws.df$lon, ws.df$lat, col=adjustcolor("black", alpha.f = 0.1))
maps::map("state", add=TRUE, col = grey(.01))

Use this model with extra care!!! Further warnings are disabled.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## read data
load("GA_data.Rdata")
load("GA_map.Rdata")
data_use$county <- as.character(data_use$county)
data_use$House_market_price <- data_use$House_market_price/1000
data_use$Population <- data_use$Population/1000
names(data_use) <- c("county", "Housing.Cost", "Unemployment.Rate",
                     "Property.Tax", "House.Market.Price", "White.Race",
                     "Age", "Population")
library(ggplot2)
GAmap <- fortify(mapdata)

library(dplyr)
long1 <- aggregate(GAmap$long, by = list(subregion = GAmap$subregion), mean)
lat1 <- aggregate(GAmap$lat, by = list(subregion = GAmap$subregion), mean)
GAdata <- data.frame("SR_ID" = c(1:159), "Latitude" = lat1$x, "Longitud" = long1$x)
GAdata <- cbind(GAdata, data_use)

## MGWR-INLA-code
library(INLA)
inla.rgeneric.beta.model <-
  function(cmd = c("graph", "Q", "mu", "initial", "log.norm.const", "log.prior", "quit"),
           theta = NULL) {
    envir = parent.env(environment())

    interpret.theta <- function() { # transform the parameters to make them unbounded
      return(list(prec = exp(theta[1L]),
                  rho = 1/(1+exp(-theta[2L])),
                  mu0 = theta[3L]))
    }
    graph <- function() {
      return (inla.as.sparse(matrix(1, n, n)))
    }
    Q <- function() { # precision matrix
      require(Matrix)
      param <- interpret.theta()
      cov.mat <- 1/param$prec * exp(-D/param$rho)
      prec.mat <- solve(cov.mat)
      return(inla.as.sparse(prec.mat))
    }
    mu <- function() {
      return (rep(interpret.theta()$mu, n))
    }
    log.norm.const <- function() {
      return (numeric())
    }
    log.prior <- function() { # log priors for the parameters of interest
      param = interpret.theta()
      res <- dgamma(param$prec, 0.01, 0.01, log = T) + log(param$prec) +
        log(1) + log(param$rho) + log(1 - param$rho) +
        dnorm(param$mu0, 0, 1, log = T)
      return(res)
    }
    initial <- function() {
      return(c(0, 0, 0))
    }
    quit <- function() {
      return(invisible())
    }

    if (!length(theta) || is.null(theta)) theta = initial()

    val <- do.call(match.arg(cmd), args = list())
    return(val)
  }

data.inla <- GAdata
# scale the variables to make the bandwidths comparable
data.inla$y <- as.vector(scale(data.inla$Housing.Cost))
data.inla$x1 <- as.vector(scale(data.inla$Unemployment.Rate))
data.inla$x2 <- as.vector(scale(data.inla$Property.Tax))
data.inla$x3 <- as.vector(scale(data.inla$House.Market.Price))
data.inla$x4 <- as.vector(scale(data.inla$White.Race))
data.inla$x5 <- as.vector(scale(data.inla$Age))
data.inla$x6 <- as.vector(scale(data.inla$Population))

Dist0 <- as.matrix(dist(data.frame(data.inla$Longitud, data.inla$Latitude)))
Dmax <- max(Dist0); Dmax
# scale the distance matrix with the maximum distance
Dist01 <- Dist0/Dmax
D <- Dist01
NN <- nrow(D); NN

# generate the self-defined function
beta.model <- inla.rgeneric.define(inla.rgeneric.beta.model,
                                   D = D,
                                   n = NN)
# model formula
f.beta <- y ~ -1 +
  f(idx1, x1, model = beta.model, n = NN) +
  f(idx2, x2, model = beta.model, n = NN) + f(idx3, x3, model = beta.model, n = NN) +
  f(idx4, x4, model = beta.model, n = NN) + f(idx5, x5, model = beta.model, n = NN) +
  f(idx6, x6, model = beta.model, n = NN)
# run the model to get the results
m.beta <- inla(f.beta,

               data = data.frame(data.inla, idx1 = 1:NN, idx2 = 1:NN, idx3 = 1:NN
                                 , idx4 = 1:NN, idx5 = 1:NN, idx6 = 1:NN),
               family = "gaussian",
               verbose = T)

messages.subject: expected value of linear predictor for different dists
messages.subject_clean: expected value of linear predictor for different dists
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

for my different models I use a Weibull, BGEV, Betabinom and Gamma distribution.
After predicting the linear predictor on a high resolution grid, I wonder how to compute the exponential value for each distribution.

For the gamma distribution I would have computed the following:

lp.mean.gamma<-unlist(lapply(lp_marg.gamma, function(x) inla.emarginal(exp, x)))

For the weibull I found in the inla.doc("weibull") that \lambda=\exp(\eta), but \lambda is not the expected value right?
For BGEV there is no real documentation and for betabinom I found that the mean equals to n*\mu_p, but I couldnt compute the corresponding command

lp.mean.betabinom<-unlist(lapply(lp_marg.betabinom, function(x) inla.emarginal(logit, x)))

Could you tell me please which functions I need to use in order to compute the mean of the respective linear predictor?

Highly appreciate your answer.

All the best,
Corinna

Even the LGCP - Distance sampling vignette <https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/web/2d_lgcp_distancesampling.html> is no longer working for me. Either it crashes or the resulting estimates are wildly incorrect if it is able to converge.

Is this issue reproducible for others with the vignette? Or is it perhaps a problem with my package installations on my end.

Cheers,
Andrew

> E_scale <- 1e5

> fit = lgcp(cmp, data = groups, formula = fml,
> domain = list(size = INLA::inla.mesh.1d(0:40,boundary=“free”)): E = E_scale )

The changes are mainly pricing a bit more specifics from the user.

messages.subject_clean: structural equation model with regression between endogenous latent variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi - I am trying to estimate structural coefficients between latent variables in an SEM using INLA/inlabru in a spatial model. Generically, I am using the LISREL notation for SEMs as follows:

y = Lambda_y*eta+epsilon
x = Lambda_x*xi+delta
eta = Beta*eta+Gamma*xi+zeta

In particular, I am trying to model the following path diagram:

Here, X1, X2 and Y1-Y4 are all point-referenced continuously-valued observations made in a particular spatial region. The lambda coefficients (at least in this model) are restricted to be 1. Epsilon, zeta and xi are all modeled as Gaussian SPDE fields with Matern covariance. Xi_1 is an exogenous latent variable, while eta_1 and eta_2 are endogenous latent variables. The intent of my modeling is to be able to estimate the gamma and beta coefficients, as well as perform assessments of model fit.

In particular, I have tried to model this as a joint model in inlabru as the following:

######

cmp <- ~
  delta_1(coordinates,model = matern) +
  delta_2(coordinates,model = matern) +
  epsilon_1(coordinates,model = matern) +
  epsilon_2(coordinates,model = matern) +
  epsilon_3(coordinates,model = matern) +
  epsilon_4(coordinates,model = matern) +
  xi_1(coordinates,model = matern) +
  zeta_1(coordinates,model = matern) +
  zeta_2(coordinates,model = matern) +
  x1_eta1(coordinates, copy = "x1_1", fixed = FALSE, hyper = hyper) +
  x1_eta2(coordinates, copy = "xi_1", fixed = FALSE, hyper = hyper) +
  zeta1_eta2(coordinates, copy = "zeta1", fixed = FALSE, hyper = hyper)

fmlas <- list(
  X1 = value ~ x1_1 + delta_1,
  X2 = value ~ x1_1 + delta_2,
  Y1 = value ~ xi1_eta1 + zeta_1 + epsilon_1,
  Y2 = value ~ x1_eta1 + zeta_1 + epsilon_2,
  Y3 = value ~ x1_eta2 + zeta1_eta2 + zeta_2 + epsilon_3,
  Y4 = value ~ x1_eta2 + zeta1_eta2 + zeta_2 + epsilon_4
)

matern <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(
  mesh = mesh,
  prior.range = c(30, 0.01), # P(range < 30) = 0.01
  prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01)) # P(sigma > 1) = 0.01
)

hyper <- list(theta = list(prior = 'normal', param = c(0, 10)))

liks <- lapply(1:length(fmlas),\(i) {

  lik <- like("gaussian",

              formula = fmlas[[i]],

              data = ds[[i]],

              domain = list(coordinates = mesh)

  )

})

# run model

args <- liks

args$components <- cmp

args$options <- list(

  control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb"),

  bru_max_iter = 1,

  bru_verbose = TRUE,

  verbose = TRUE

)

fit <- do.call(bru,args)

#####

After fitting this model, the gamma coefficients can be read off easily, as they are explicitly modeled, since they model connections from an exogenous latent variable to an endogenous latent variable.

However, the beta coefficients are a little trickier - do you have any thoughts on how the beta coefficients may be estimated? That is, are there any thoughts on how (essentially) a regression of an endogenous latent variable on another endogenous latent variable can be performed? I have seen some evidence of this being performed in other Bayesian packages such as brms encoding the latent variable as a variable with missing values (for example, here <https://scottclaessens.github.io/blog/2020/brmsLV/>), but am unsure if this is the right approach, or how I could do this in INLA.

Thanks for any help or guidance! I am rather new to INLA/inlabru, as well as SEMs, so any assistance you can provide or mistakes you can point out would be greatly appreciated!

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] expected value of linear predictor for different dists
messages.body_plain:
it would be easier to compute quantiles, as you can just pass them
through...

for the BGEV the expected values has less meaning, and I would suggest
using a quantile instead (see the original bgev-paper for that)

If you really want the exected value, then you can compute it two ways,

for example, let z=exp(x),  we have have density for x and want the
expected value for z.

1. compute the density for z, using inla.tmarginal, then compute the
expected value for 'z' using inla.emarginal, or inla.zmarginal

2. compute the expected value of exp(x) (wrt to the density of x), using
inla.emarginal.

approach 2 is more stable.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] structural equation model with regression between endogenous latent variables
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] structural equation model with regression between endogenous latent variables
messages.body_plain:
Yes - eta and xi are both latent variables. xi are exogenous (do not depend on other latents), while eta are endogenous (other latent variables can be inputs to them). Beta controls the (linear) mapping between endogenous variables. Most generally, Beta can allow for feedback loops, but I am not interested in this case (thus Beta can be permuted to be strictly upper-diagonal).

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] defining uniform prior for the hyperparameter
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] defining uniform prior for the hyperparameter
messages.body_plain:
you cannot define a bounded interval, also, there is not good reason for
doing that in my opinion.

you can define PC-prior,

https://projecteuclid.org/journals/statistical-science/volume-32/issue-1/Penalising-Model-Component-Complexity--A-Principled-Practical-Approach-to/10.1214/16-STS576.full

f(.., model="iid", hyper=list(prec=list(prior="pc.prec"param=c(A,0.01)))

then hyperpar is prec=1/sigma^2

	Prob(sigma > A) = 0.01

and

	SD(iid.effect) \approx 0.3*A

after prior is integrated out.

the prior is exponential, so with higher A, the rate is low, hence
alomost uniform.

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone

Just out of curiosity while running the joint model I tried executing the following

formula for a model where both structured and unstructured random effects of one data set is shared to another
formula=Y~0+Inter+ f(ID.shared1, model="bym", graph=g1) + f(ID.shared2, copy= 'ID.shared1', model="bym",graph=g1) + f(ID2, model="bym", graph=g)
this runs well.

Similarly when i just tried if i could share the spatial random effect fitted using leroux model I got error
formula2=Y~0+Inter+ f(ID.shared1, model="generic1", Cmatrix = C1)+ f(ID.shared2, copy= 'ID.shared1', model="generic1", Cmatrix = C1) + f(ID2, model="generic1", Cmatrix = C2)

Error is :
Error in INLA::f(ID.shared2, copy = "ID.shared1", model = "generic1",  :
  Cmatrix is not used for this model: copy
Error in inla.core.safe(formula = formula, family = family, contrasts = contrasts,  :
  *** Fail to get good enough initial values. Maybe it is due to something else.

Is this approach is not theoretically valid?

For “copy” models, one cannot change the structure of the model component being copied; the other arguments, like model and graph are probably ignored, but it happened to notice you tried to change the Cmatrix and complained.  Leave out the extra arguments when defining your copies, and it should work.

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] inla.mode options
messages.body_plain:
inla.hyperpar is for 'classic' only.

for the default mode, there is not way to improve the hyperparameters
estimates.

we're working on a series of variational Bayes corrections, and we have
done the mean (default), variance (not default) and we're working on the
skewness for the latent field. Next one after that is
hyperparameters....

messages.body_plain:
Interesting discussion that I have been bouncing around for about two years. Just on the constr = F discussion, my results are definitely looking dodgy whenever I set constr = T

set.seed(3.141)

library(ape)
library(mvtnorm)
library(phytools)
library(INLA)
library(ggplot2)
library(brms)

tmp_tr = pbtree(n = 20) #Generate a random tree of 20 tips
cov = vcv.phylo(tmp_tr, corr = T) #Produce a covariance matrix scaled to a maximum of 1
rownames(cov) = c(1:20) #Index the matrix with numbers instead of tip names
colnames(cov) = c(1:20)
coef = data.frame(
  id = c(1:20),
  vec = as.vector(rmvnorm(1, rep(0,20), cov))) #Simulate data from this covariance
sd(coef$vec) #Look at the standard deviation of this simulated data
phylosig(tmp_tr, coef$vec, method = "lambda") #Test phylogentic signal in the simulated data - its high (big surprise...)!

#Use the simulated coefficients to produce random slopes with a degree of error
cmb_df = NULL
for(a in 1:20){
  tmp_df = data.frame(
    x = 1:10,
    y = c(1:10)*coef$vec[a] + rnorm(10,0,2),
    group = a)
  cmb_df = rbind(cmb_df, tmp_df)
}

#Visualise the data - some very variable slopes on show. The whole premise of this analaysis is that we expect slopes to be more similar in closely related species, and this needs to be accounted for when trying to derive an estimate for the y ~ x slope (the parameter we are most interested  in)
ggplot(cmb_df) +
  geom_line(aes(x = x, y = y, group = group))

prec = solve(cov) #COnvert the correlation matrix into a precision matrix

pcprior = list(prec = list(
  prior="pc.prec",
  param = c(10, 0.1))
) #Simple pc prior

#The first model we is a simple random slope model with an iid model sturucture
inla_iid = inla(y ~ x +
                  f(group,
                    x,
                    model = "iid",
                    constr = T,
                    hyper = pcprior),
                data = cmb_df,
                control.family = list(hyper = pcprior))
summary(inla_iid) #95% CIs around x vary from 0.45 - 0.64

#Same model as above, but without the pc prior. This difference in prior should cause small discrepancies in the outputs.
brm_iid <- brm(
  y ~ x + (x|group),
  data = cmb_df,
  family = gaussian(),
  chains = 1
)
summary(brm_iid) #95% CIs around x vary from 0.20 - 0.87. Quite different, but perhaps that's just because of differences in the prior... bare with me, as I'm not really interested in the absolute difference between inla and brms. But how different options in inla change things (or not)

#Now we specify that the precision matrix from the phylogeny should describe the slopes (e.g. slopes exhibit phylo signal). Our expectation here would be that, by addressing non-independence in slopes, our uncertainty around the y ~ x relationship should increase
inla_constrT = inla(y ~ x +
                      f(group,
                        x,
                        model = "generic0",
                        Cmatrix = prec,
                        constr = T,
                        hyper = pcprior),
                    data = cmb_df,
                    control.family = list(hyper = pcprior))
summary(inla_constrT) #But no! We have an identical estimate to the simple random slope model (0.45 - 0.64)

brm_cov <- brm(
  y ~ x + (x|gr(group, cov = A)),
  data = cmb_df,
  family = gaussian(),
  data2 = list(A = cov),,
  chains = 1
)
summary(brm_cov) #In constract, with brms the 95% CI is now -0.44 - 1.58. The standard deviation around the y ~ x relationship is now almost an order of magnitude greater than INLA, and nearly three times larger than the initial brms model

#Interestingly, if we re-run the phylogentic inla model, but set constr = F, the result all of a sudden become more comparable to brms again
inla_constrF = inla(y ~ x +
                      f(group,
                        x,
                        model = "generic0",
                        Cmatrix = prec,
                        constr = F,
                        hyper = pcprior),
                    data = cmb_df,
                    control.family = list(hyper = pcprior))
summary(inla_constrF) #95% CIs range from -0.82 - 1.96

#And importantly, are comparable to what we would expect based on our simulation
print(quantile(coef$vec, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)))

#I have no idea what is going on under the hood here, but setting constr = T seems to screw with inference. Constr = F feels far more reliable despite all of the advice disagreeing with this. I would love it if someone could explain what is going on here

On Wednesday, 18 May 2022 at 14:35:31 UTC+1 Russell Dinnage wrote:
> Hi Richard,
>
> Thanks very much for getting back to me. This is very helpful feedback. I think the issue with the intercept is an interesting one. Out of curiosity, in your simulations, did you always assume the root value was zero? Using constr = TRUE is necessary to make the intercept identifiable, so when they say the model is more 'stable', it means that the estimate of the intercept is not too strongly influenced by its prior. Note that the default prior is centred at zero, so it is possible when you set contr = FALSE the model was giving the correct intercept estimate because it happened to be that zero was the correct answer. However, setting constr = TRUE is forcing a constraint that is not biologically realistic, that is, there is no reason that the evolutionary process would have necessarily led to deviations in the traits that exactly cancel each other to zero. I think the overall issue is that the Brownian motion phylogenetic model is overall just weakly identified. Afterall it is implicitly estimating (n + (n-1)) rate parameters for n effective data points. With the gaussian restriction the effective parameters is lower than that, but if you look at the effective number of parameters estimated by INLA for the Brownian motion model, it is typically between n/2 and n, so there is generally an effective sample size of less than 2. So expecting it to accurately estimate both the intercept (e.g. ancestral state at the root), and all the evolutionary rates is asking a bit much.
>
> My understanding of "generic2" is that the first parameter is the precision on the phylogenetic effect, the second parameter the precision of the "environmental effect", e.g. the iid 'random noise' component, which should be equivalent to the gaussian error precision term when using a "generic0" gaussian model. This is why you need to fix the gaussian error term in the "generic2" model, otherwise you have two iid terms. I notice in the code you posted you didn't fix the family error precision term, so this may be why the results were different between the two models. Anyway, it sounds like you have moved from the INLA models for the time being, so I suppose we should leave it at that. Just FYI, I am working on an R package that will be able to fit flexible phylogenetic models in INLA, with a user-friendly interface that you might be interested in. I should be doing an initial release within the next month or so. If you are interested I can keep you posted on that?
>
> All the best,
> Russell
>
>
> On Mon, 16 May 2022 at 09:28, Richard Bailey <richardi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Russell,
> >
> > Thanks for getting in touch, and sorry to be slow to reply - just back from fieldwork. The current state of play is that I switched back to using MCMCglmm, as I know the package so much better and I don't have enough time to sort out all the question marks I have in my mind to be confident enough to use INLA/phyr. Initially I wanted to use INLA because it includes beta family, which MCMCglmm doesn't have, but I've decided to just logit-transform the proportions instead. I'll try to answer your questions, although I may mis-remember some details as it's a few months since I ran the analyses.
> >
> > In terms of testing the methods, I made a very simple set of simulated datasets using MCMCglmm::rbv, exactly following the example code for that function, which no doubt uses the root-tip=1 scaling. I don't remember what else I did with respect to simulating data. I then fitted an intercept only model with just the inverted phylogeny as a random effect.
> >
> > The biggest issue, if I remember correctly, was that in phyr, the Bayesian=TRUE and Bayesian=FALSE models produced results for the intercept that were not comparable (I can't remember if there were differences in the random effects variance/precision estimates), and while the non-Bayesian model confidence intervals overlapped as expected with the true value for the intercept, the Bayesian credible intervals did not. (Again, apologies if I'm mis-remembering something) One issue I found when I followed up, using INLA directly, was that, within the f() argument, there is an option "constr=TRUE/FALSE". When this is set to TRUE (as it is ?? for phyr ??) the fixed effects credible intervals were tight around the sample mean, and rarely overlapped with the true value. Whereas when I changed this to "constr=FALSE", the credible intervals were much wider and usually overlapped with the true value. Maybe "constr=TRUE" produces better random effects precision estimates (I think with animalINLA they used this option because they said it's more 'stable')? But for using the model to control for non-independence when estimating fixed effects, it seems like it should be "constr=FALSE". I have no idea what this option is doing...
> >
> >
> > > Reading the paper linked to in animalINLA, my interpretation is that the "generic2" and "generic0" setup are equivalent accept that the "generic2" makes it easier to estimate the derived h^2 heritability parameter (which is rarely used in phylogenetic analyses in my experience). The paper also claims "generic2" setup does not give correct DIC measures but "generic0" does. Since model comparison is of interest in phyr, so far I am leaning towards keeping that formulation. In your experience have you found any other benefits of using "generic2"? I don't know if the same issue applies to WAIC though, which I prefer to use over DIC anyway. Anyone here know about this?
> >
> > This was also my interpretation of "generic2", but when I ran it, I always got different estimates for the first parameter (which I assume to be the precision of the random effect) than for the single parameter using "generic0". So, I'm not sure if my understanding of the second parameter was correct.
> >
> > I'm also unclear on whether "generic0" is equivalent to fitting the matrix inverse in MCMCglmm, which according to Hadfield, is equivalent to assuming brownian motion evolution along a phylogeny.
> >
> > One other potential issue with making an equivalent model with INLA to the MCMCglmm model (which was my original intention, and the main reason I posted a question) is that INLA estimates precision whereas MCMCglmm estimates variance, so I doubt (though I haven't verified) it would be possible to create equivalent priors. I never got as far as figuring out how to set the priors, I just used defaults.
> >
> > > I wanted to ask what you meant by the scaling used in the phyr example leading to "incorrect" estimates? Incorrect estimates of the fixed effects?

> >
> > > Note that phyr also uses MCMCglmm::inverseA internally to calculate the correct precision matrix, however, at the moment we use the tips-only option. I also came to the conclusion some time ago that we should use the whole phylogeny, including internal nodes to calculate the precision matrix, and include missing data for the internal nodes. This as mentioned above should be more accurate but I have also found for large phylogenies it is orders of magnitude faster, presumably because the full precision matrix is sparse, whereas the tips-only covariance matrix is dense, and INLA is very efficient for sparse matrices (this still seems very counter-intuitive to me, but I have been convinced by experience that it is true).
> >

Apparently, in MCMCglmm this improves mixing of the MCMC and leads to higher effective sampling with fewer iterations. In MCMCglmm it's completely straightforward, the internal nodes (and also any species in the phylogeny with no response data) are just treated automatically as missing response data, and their values can be predicted post hoc via the phylogenetic relationships.
> >
> > > Anyway, I have not yet had the time to implement this change in phyr yet partly because the main effects of interest in phyr are the 'nested' phylogenetic effects, which actually use the Kronecker product of the phylogenetic covariance and an iid covariance for the "sites", and I need to think carefully about how to do this correctly with the internal nodes (it is probably not as complicated as I think). I have been wondering for awhile whether I could use the "group" argument of f() to accomplish an equivalent model, but haven't had time to look into it properly. If anyone has any thought on this, I would love to hear them!
> >
> > I've tried something similar with MCMCglmm and it also works fine without any special adjustments when including internal nodes - I guess the non-existent site:internal node combinations are just treated as missing response data like before (they exist in the kronecker product matrix, so as predictors they're not missing). I don't know if it's equally straightforward with INLA.
> >
> > Thanks again for your feedback, best wishes,
> >
> > Richard.

> > > > > > > > > You must not subset your precision matrix (Ainv)! Doing this destroys the model structure, since precision matrix is indicating conditional model structure. You can subset covariance matrix (this indicates marginal model structure) and invert it if you want, but given that we can setup the phylogenetic precision matrix directly I see no point in doing this.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Gregor
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > On Wednesday, August 18, 2021 at 1:35:11 PM UTC+1 Richard Bailey wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > Hi,
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > I'm currently trying to replicate the following MCMCglmm model using INLA, but without success so far. The objective is to estimate the coefficients of effects of 'fixed effect' predictors on the response while controlling for non-independence among data points (species) due to their evolutionary relationships ('phylogeny'). According to a Brownian motion model, which I'm assuming, the covariance among data points (species) drops linearly and proportionally with increasing distance in evolutionary time.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > A phylogeny in this case is an ultrametric bifurcating representation of evolutionary distances in time ('branch lengths') among species, with tips (the individual species) connected by internal nodes (which also connect to each other via other nodes), and a root node connecting everything. Branch lengths vary among each pair of connecting nodes and tips, but all tips are the same distance from the root.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > #############################################
> > > > > > > > > > #Example MCMCglmm analysis setup on a simulated dataset#
> > > > > > > > > > #############################################
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > library(MCMCglmm);
> > > > > > > > > > data(bird.families);#This is a representation of the phylogenetic relationships among bird families (although I refer to 'species' elsewhere, in this example it's families)#
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > #Simulate some data
> > > > > > > > > > set.seed(123456)
> > > > > > > > > > phylo.effect<-MCMCglmm::rbv(bird.families, 1, nodes="TIPS")#"Random Generation of MVN Breeding Values and Phylogenetic Effects". "TIPS" are the families - we don't have trait values for internal nodes. The '1' here refers to the variance of the simulated values#
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > set.seed(23456)
> > > > > > > > > > phenotype<-phylo.effect+rnorm(dim(phylo.effect)[1], 0, 1)#Adding the non-phylogenetic component of trait variation#
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > test.data<-data.frame(phenotype=phenotype, taxon=row.names(phenotype))
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > #Create a sparse inverse matrix of the phylogeny#
> > > > > > > > > >  Ainv<-MCMCglmm::inverseA(bird.families)$Ainv#This includes all tips (species) and internal nodes (for the latter we have no trait data)#
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > #Run the analysis#
> > > > > > > > > > prior<-list(R=list(V=1, nu=0.002), G=list(G1=list(V=1, nu=0.002)));
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > model<-MCMCglmm(phenotype~1, random=~taxon, ginverse=list(taxon=Ainv), data=test.data, prior=prior);
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > This estimates the intercept and the phylogenetic and residual variance components. The estimate and uncertainty of the intercept in this model are modified due to the non-zero phylogenetic random effect for bird families.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > I've tried several INLA model setups to replicate this, but without success. These include copying the animalINLA model setup, with either model="generic0" or model="generic2", and with the inverse matrix for the bird families input using Cmatrix (including only tips, but created by subsetting the Ainv object above to just tips, rather than inverting the matrix based on tips alone; according to MCMCglmm documentation this would seem to be okay). Here's the model:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > inla(phenotype~f(spN, model="generic2", hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(0.5, 0.5), fixed = FALSE),theta2 = list(param = c(0.5, 0.5), fixed = FALSE)), constr = TRUE, Cmatrix = AinvSM) + 1,data=testdata,control.family = list(hyper = list(theta = list(initial = 10, fixed = TRUE))));
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > I'm totally guessing here, but I wonder if INLA is assuming that the bird families are equidistant in evolutionary time? I used numeric 1:N families as rownames in Cmatrix, and made an equivalent numeric variable in the data table (spN) to cross reference with it. But if INLA is assuming equidistance, what is the purpose of the Cmatrix?
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > I compared MCMCglmm with INLA (using the animalINLA setup with "generic2" as above) for the intercept and phylogeny random effect using 100 datasets simulated as above. I found that the intercept means were at least proportional (with r^2=0.5) but with much narrower credible intervals in INLA, almost exclusively non-overlapping with the true population value. For the phylogenetic random effect, there is a relationship between the MCMCglmm and INLA estimates (r^2~0.2) but it's more noisy and not proportional (slope~0.5).
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > If I've done something completely wrong please let me know!
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > I see there have been related questions previously, but so far I don't have the impression there's a conclusive answer.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Many thanks for your time!
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > All the best, Richard.
> > > > > > > > > >

messages.body_plain:
There is no correct choice of using constr=T or F, its up to you.

with

	~ ... + x + f(group, x, model="iid", constr=T or F)

then with 'T' you'll get sum(group)=0, but what you might want is the
weigted sum to be 0, so that

	x + f()

has the interpretation of 'mean slope + variations around'.

if you know the weights, you can use 'extraconstr' instead.

It think the main issue is the variance of 'x' and f(), as without
constr they can be higher due to confounding, but with some data I think
the effect is small.

H

On Thu, 2023-06-15 at 04:41 -0700, 'Thomas F Johnson' via R-inla

discussion group wrote:
> Interesting discussion that I have been bouncing around for about two
> years. Just on the constr = F discussion, my results are definitely

> set.seed(3.141)

> library(ape)

>
> tmp_tr = pbtree(n = 20) #Generate a random tree of 20 tips

>
>

>

>
>

>

>                   f(group,

>                     model = "iid",
>                     constr = T,

>   chains = 1
> )
> summary(brm_iid) #95% CIs around x vary from 0.20 - 0.87. Quite

>
> #Now we specify that the precision matrix from the phylogeny should

> simple random slope model (0.45 - 0.64)
>
> brm_cov <- brm(
>   y ~ x + (x|gr(group, cov = A)),
>   data = cmb_df,
>   family = gaussian(),
>   data2 = list(A = cov),,
>   chains = 1
> )
> summary(brm_cov) #In constract, with brms the 95% CI is now -0.44 -
> 1.58. The standard deviation around the y ~ x relationship is now
> almost an order of magnitude greater than INLA, and nearly three times

>
> #Interestingly, if we re-run the phylogentic inla model, but set
> constr = F, the result all of a sudden become more comparable to brms
> again
> inla_constrF = inla(y ~ x +
>                       f(group,
>                         x,
>                         model = "generic0",
>                         Cmatrix = prec,
>                         constr = F,
>                         hyper = pcprior),
>                     data = cmb_df,
>                     control.family = list(hyper = pcprior))
> summary(inla_constrF) #95% CIs range from -0.82 - 1.96
>
> #And importantly, are comparable to what we would expect based on our
> simulation
> print(quantile(coef$vec, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)))
>
> #I have no idea what is going on under the hood here, but setting
> constr = T seems to screw with inference. Constr = F feels far more
> reliable despite all of the advice disagreeing with this. I would love

> On Wednesday, 18 May 2022 at 14:35:31 UTC+1 Russell Dinnage wrote:
> > Hi Richard,
> >
> > Thanks very much for getting back to me. This is very helpful
> > feedback. I think the issue with the intercept is an interesting
> > one. Out of curiosity, in your simulations, did you always assume
> > the root value was zero? Using constr = TRUE is necessary to make
> > the intercept identifiable, so when they say the model is more
> > 'stable', it means that the estimate of the intercept is not too
> > strongly influenced by its prior. Note that the default prior is
> > centred at zero, so it is possible when you set contr = FALSE the
> > model was giving the correct intercept estimate because it happened
> > to be that zero was the correct answer. However, setting constr =
> > TRUE is forcing a constraint that is not biologically realistic,
> > that is, there is no reason that the evolutionary process would have
> > necessarily led to deviations in the traits that exactly cancel each
> > other to zero. I think the overall issue is that the Brownian motion
> > phylogenetic model is overall just weakly identified. Afterall it is
> > implicitly estimating (n + (n-1)) rate parameters for n effective
> > data points. With the gaussian restriction the effective parameters
> > is lower than that, but if you look at the effective number of
> > parameters estimated by INLA for the Brownian motion model, it is
> > typically between n/2 and n, so there is generally an effective
> > sample size of less than 2. So expecting it to accurately estimate
> > both the intercept (e.g. ancestral state at the root), and all the
> > evolutionary rates is asking a bit much.
> >
> > My understanding of "generic2" is that the first parameter is the
> > precision on the phylogenetic effect, the second parameter the
> > precision of the "environmental effect", e.g. the iid 'random noise'
> > component, which should be equivalent to the gaussian error
> > precision term when using a "generic0" gaussian model. This is why
> > you need to fix the gaussian error term in the "generic2" model,
> > otherwise you have two iid terms. I notice in the code you posted
> > you didn't fix the family error precision term, so this may be why
> > the results were different between the two models. Anyway, it sounds
> > like you have moved from the INLA models for the time being, so I
> > suppose we should leave it at that. Just FYI, I am working on an R
> > package that will be able to fit flexible phylogenetic models in
> > INLA, with a user-friendly interface that you might be interested
> > in. I should be doing an initial release within the next month or
> > so. If you are interested I can keep you posted on that?
> >
> > All the best,
> > Russell
> >
> >
> > On Mon, 16 May 2022 at 09:28, Richard Bailey <richardi...@gmail.com>
> > wrote:
> > > Hi Russell,
> > >
> > > Thanks for getting in touch, and sorry to be slow to reply - just
> > > back from fieldwork. The current state of play is that I switched

> > > don't have enough time to sort out all the question marks I
> > > have in my mind to be confident enough to use INLA/phyr. Initially
> > > I wanted to use INLA because it includes beta family, which
> > > MCMCglmm doesn't have, but I've decided to just logit-transform
> > > the proportions instead. I'll try to answer your questions,
> > > although I may mis-remember some details as it's a few months
> > > since I ran the analyses.
> > >
> > > In terms of testing the methods, I made a very simple set of
> > > simulated datasets using MCMCglmm::rbv, exactly following the
> > > example code for that function, which no doubt uses the root-tip=1
> > > scaling. I don't remember what else I did with respect to
> > > simulating data. I then fitted an intercept only model with just
> > > the inverted phylogeny as a random effect.
> > >
> > > The biggest issue, if I remember correctly, was that in phyr, the
> > > Bayesian=TRUE and Bayesian=FALSE models produced results for the
> > > intercept that were not comparable (I can't remember if there were
> > > differences in the random effects variance/precision estimates),
> > > and while the non-Bayesian model confidence intervals overlapped
> > > as expected with the true value for the intercept, the Bayesian

> > > remembering something) One issue I found when I followed up, using
> > > INLA directly, was that, within the f() argument, there is an

> > > precision estimates (I think with animalINLA they used this option

> > > control for non-independence when estimating fixed effects, it
> > > seems like it should be "constr=FALSE". I have no idea what this
> > > option is doing...
> > >
> > >
> > > > Reading the paper linked to in animalINLA, my interpretation is
> > > > that the "generic2" and "generic0" setup are equivalent accept
> > > > that the "generic2" makes it easier to estimate the derived h^2

> > > This was also my interpretation of "generic2", but when I ran it,

> > > assume to be the precision of the random effect) than for the
> > > single parameter using "generic0". So, I'm not sure if my
> > > understanding of the second parameter was correct.
> > >
> > > I'm also unclear on whether "generic0" is equivalent to fitting

> > >
> > > One other potential issue with making an equivalent model with
> > > INLA to the MCMCglmm model (which was my original intention, and
> > > the main reason I posted a question) is that INLA estimates
> > > precision whereas MCMCglmm estimates variance, so I doubt (though
> > > I haven't verified) it would be possible to create equivalent

> > >
> > > > I wanted to ask what you meant by the scaling used in the phyr
> > > > example leading to "incorrect" estimates? Incorrect estimates of

> > >
> > > I'm trying to remember why I used the word "incorrect". Maybe I

> > > correct one, and that the one you suggested ought to be doing the
> > > same.
> > >
> > > > Note that phyr also uses MCMCglmm::inverseA internally to
> > > > calculate the correct precision matrix, however, at the moment
> > > > we use the tips-only option. I also came to the conclusion some
> > > > time ago that we should use the whole phylogeny, including
> > > > internal nodes to calculate the precision matrix, and include
> > > > missing data for the internal nodes. This as mentioned above
> > > > should be more accurate but I have also found for large
> > > > phylogenies it is orders of magnitude faster, presumably because
> > > > the full precision matrix is sparse, whereas the tips-only
> > > > covariance matrix is dense, and INLA is very efficient for
> > > > sparse matrices (this still seems very counter-intuitive to me,
> > > > but I have been convinced by experience that it is true).
> > >
> > > Yes, I think the improvement is because including the internal
> > > nodes makes the precision matrix sparse. Apparently, in MCMCglmm
> > > this improves mixing of the MCMC and leads to higher effective
> > > sampling with fewer iterations. In MCMCglmm it's completely
> > > straightforward, the internal nodes (and also any species in the

> > >
> > > >  Anyway, I have not yet had the time to implement this change in
> > > > phyr yet partly because the main effects of interest in phyr are
> > > > the 'nested' phylogenetic effects, which actually use the
> > > > Kronecker product of the phylogenetic covariance and an iid
> > > > covariance for the "sites", and I need to think carefully about
> > > > how to do this correctly with the internal nodes (it is probably
> > > > not as complicated as I think). I have been wondering for awhile
> > > > whether I could use the "group" argument of f() to accomplish an
> > > > equivalent model, but haven't had time to look into it properly.
> > > > If anyone has any thought on this, I would love to hear them!
> > >
> > > I've tried something similar with MCMCglmm and it also works fine
> > > without any special adjustments when including internal nodes - I
> > > guess the non-existent site:internal node combinations are just
> > > treated as missing response data like before (they exist in the
> > > kronecker product matrix, so as predictors they're not missing). I
> > > don't know if it's equally straightforward with INLA.
> > >
> > > Thanks again for your feedback, best wishes,
> > >
> > > Richard.
> > >

messages.body_plain:
Hi Thomas,

(I know you know a lot of this stuff already, but in case anyone else is reading and wants to know the objectives of these analyses).

I haven't gone through your email in detail, but regarding constr=T, what I found specifically was that my fixed-effect posterior estimates of the intercept (true value the data were simulated from = zero) were centred on the sample mean, with very tight credible intervals. Therefore, they didn't overlap with the true value of the intercept (0). Whatever is causing this outcome, it is unhelpful for standard phylogenetically informed comparative analysis. The typical objective is to incorporate the increased uncertainty due to correlations (evolutionary non-independence) among data points - reducing the effective number of data points - into estimation of fixed-effect parameters. Sometimes the objective is to estimate the phylogenetic variance components, but that's not how most people use this method - they are focused on dealing with the statistical non-independence issue while estimating fixed effects.

For me, setting constr=F produced results that made far more sense, with increased uncertainty in the intercept estimate compared to the non-phylogenetic model, and credible intervals from almost all simulated datasets overlapping with the true value (0). I didn't try adding any more fixed effects, or using a different intercept than zero.

Best regards,
Richard.

> > Thanks very much for getting back to me. This is very helpful feedback. I think the issue with the intercept is an interesting one. Out of curiosity, in your simulations, did you always assume the root value was zero? Using constr = TRUE is necessary to make the intercept identifiable, so when they say the model is more 'stable', it means that the estimate of the intercept is not too strongly influenced by its prior. Note that the default prior is centred at zero, so it is possible when you set contr = FALSE the model was giving the correct intercept estimate because it happened to be that zero was the correct answer. However, setting constr = TRUE is forcing a constraint that is not biologically realistic, that is, there is no reason that the evolutionary process would have necessarily led to deviations in the traits that exactly cancel each other to zero. I think the overall issue is that the Brownian motion phylogenetic model is overall just weakly identified. Afterall it is implicitly estimating (n + (n-1)) rate parameters for n effective data points. With the gaussian restriction the effective parameters is lower than that, but if you look at the effective number of parameters estimated by INLA for the Brownian motion model, it is typically between n/2 and n, so there is generally an effective sample size of less than 2. So expecting it to accurately estimate both the intercept (e.g. ancestral state at the root), and all the evolutionary rates is asking a bit much.

This is why you need to fix the gaussian error term in the "generic2" model, otherwise you have two iid terms. I notice in the code you posted you didn't fix the family error precision term, so this may be why the results were different between the two models. > > > > > > > > > > > set.seed(123456)
> > > > > > > > > > > phylo.effect<-MCMCglmm::rbv(bird.families, 1, nodes="TIPS")#"Random Generation of MVN Breeding Values and Phylogenetic Effects". "TIPS" are the families - we don't have trait values for internal nodes. The '1' here refers to the variance of the simulated values#
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > set.seed(23456)
> > > > > > > > > > > phenotype<-phylo.effect+rnorm(dim(phylo.effect)[1], 0, 1)#Adding the non-phylogenetic component of trait variation#
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > test.data<-data.frame(phenotype=phenotype, taxon=row.names(phenotype))
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > #Create a sparse inverse matrix of the phylogeny#
> > > > > > > > > > >  Ainv<-MCMCglmm::inverseA(bird.families)$Ainv#This includes all tips (species) and internal nodes (for the latter we have no trait data)#
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > #Run the analysis#
> > > > > > > > > > > prior<-list(R=list(V=1, nu=0.002), G=list(G1=list(V=1, nu=0.002)));
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > model<-MCMCglmm(phenotype~1, random=~taxon, ginverse=list(taxon=Ainv), data=test.data, prior=prior);
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > This estimates the intercept and the phylogenetic and residual variance components. The estimate and uncertainty of the intercept in this model are modified due to the non-zero phylogenetic random effect for bird families.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > I've tried several INLA model setups to replicate this, but without success. These include copying the animalINLA model setup, with either model="generic0" or model="generic2", and with the inverse matrix for the bird families input using Cmatrix (including only tips, but created by subsetting the Ainv object above to just tips, rather than inverting the matrix based on tips alone; according to MCMCglmm documentation this would seem to be okay). Here's the model:
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > inla(phenotype~f(spN, model="generic2", hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(0.5, 0.5), fixed = FALSE),theta2 = list(param = c(0.5, 0.5), fixed = FALSE)), constr = TRUE, Cmatrix = AinvSM) + 1,data=testdata,control.family = list(hyper = list(theta = list(initial = 10, fixed = TRUE))));
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > I'm totally guessing here, but I wonder if INLA is assuming that the bird families are equidistant in evolutionary time? I used numeric 1:N families as rownames in Cmatrix, and made an equivalent numeric variable in the data table (spN) to cross reference with it. But if INLA is assuming equidistance, what is the purpose of the Cmatrix?
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > I compared MCMCglmm with INLA (using the animalINLA setup with "generic2" as above) for the intercept and phylogeny random effect using 100 datasets simulated as above. I found that the intercept means were at least proportional (with r^2=0.5) but with much narrower credible intervals in INLA, almost exclusively non-overlapping with the true population value. For the phylogenetic random effect, there is a relationship between the MCMCglmm and INLA estimates (r^2~0.2) but it's more noisy and not proportional (slope~0.5).
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > If I've done something completely wrong please let me know!
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > I see there have been related questions previously, but so far I don't have the impression there's a conclusive answer.
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > Many thanks for your time!
> > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > All the best, Richard.

messages.subject_clean: Prior on scaling parameter to shrink towards zero
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I would like to fit a preferential model such as:

~ ... + f(field_pp, model=...) + f(field_mark_copypp, copy = "spde_pp" , fixed = F, hyper = list( beta=... )) + f( field_mark2, model=...)

where beta shrinks towards zero. In other words, I want the model to somehow neglect "field_mark_copypp" when the data is not really preferentially sampled, i.e. "field_pp" does not resemble the actual field of the marks.

So far I have unsuccesfuly tried these two:
 gaussian prior --> list(prior = 'gaussian', param = c(0, .051))
and a pc.prior --> list(theta = list(prior = "pc.prior",  param = c(0, 1e-9),
    initial = c(0, 0))
Both the mark and the pp use log links. May this be why the above dont work?
Any suggestions?

Cheers,
iosu

Thanks for your fast reply Finn! Yes, it is an error sorry.it <http://sorry.it> should be "field_pp" as well.

Sorry for not explaining well enough my problem. By "dont work" I meant that when I draw a random sample (homogeneous pp), field_pp is not a flat function because it draws information from the marks when fitting the shared field  field_mark_copypp. As a results field_mark_copypp + field_mark2 does resemble the marks function, but the Poin Pattern field (field_pp ) is far from realistic.

My though was that, if I were able to put a strong prior on the scaling parameter to shrink towards zero, field_pp could be realistic (konstant) and have a minimal impact on the marks function. And consequentely, field_mark2 alone would resemble the marks function.

cheers,
Iosu

messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

would be easier to test with basic calls to inla() or fmesher code to
rule out any issues with the input data, and it might give clearer
error messages.

fit <- inla(y~1, data = data.frame(y = rnorm(10)), family="normal",
verbose=TRUE)

and

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(cbind(0,0), offset = 1, max.edge = 2)

In your case, you might also check if you can build the experimental
fmesher package, with
  remotes::install_github("inlabru-org/fmesher")
and try
  fmesher::fmesher_rcdt(list(),loc=cbind(0,0))
It doesn't have the functionality you need yet, but might help
identify a build problem.

Finn

So it's unclear to me now why they are not working in my codes:

messages.body_plain:
OK, that's a good start, as being able to run both inla() and
inla.mesh.2d() indicates the build itself is working.
I haven't changed the fmesher code in INLA in a while (although the
build methods and settings may have changed).

The "missing manifold" happens both when fmesher crashes and when the
generated mesh is empty (for whatever reason), e.g. due to the
boundary specification defining an empty mesh, or some other input
data problem.
So I'd first check the inputs your code is using for the mesh generator.

Finn

I wanted to know if the Inla.mesh.2d function changes the data projection.
That is to say that to be able to do the prior range on the SPDE you have to know the unit of spatial measurement, if I understood correctly.

But only on internet I can't get confirmation of whether it keeps the crs specified as input to the mesh or whether it goes back to a particular projection.
To create my mesh I use location from a WGS84 projection. So I specify this in the crs input.
I wonder in view of the image that comes out a little flattened compared to a WGS84 representation, if it will not project the data to have something correctly positioned.

If someone have the answer ?

Thank you,
Aurel Hebert Burggraeve

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inla.mesh.2d spatial projection
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] inla.mesh.2d spatial projection
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the safest way in "pure" INLA is to transform the observations to be
on the same crs as the mesh to be absolutely sure the data is mapped
correctly to the mesh.  The spde model is always built in the
coordinate system the mesh is stored in, so if you specified a crs  to
inla.mesh.2d, that's the coordinate system (and unit of measurements)
for the model. There is partial support for doing automated mapping
between different crs:es when evaluating results with the help of the
inla.mesh.project/or() methods.

However, I would strongly recommend shifting to using the tools
currently in the inlabru package for this instead, as those will very
soon replace the methods currently in the inla package; the
inlabru::fm_evaluate() and inlabru::fm_evaluator() methods have full
support for automatically translating between different crs:es, both
for 'sp' and 'sf' objects.

If you're running models in inlabru as well, then this support extends
to the data-predictor-component links (at least if you're using sf
data with comp(geometry, ...); the comp(coordinates, ...) approach
drops crs info, so with sp you're again safer by first converting the
data to the same crs as the mesh, e.g. using fm_transform()), so that
observations and the spde model do not need to be on the same crs.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I had missed the previous question.

When the covariate is on a finer scale than the mesh, I tend to do this:

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=covariategridlocations)

Covariateonmesh<-(Covariatevalues %*% A) / colSums(A)

This evaluates locally weighted averages of the covariates, using the mesh basis functions as weights.

Finn

Thank you very much Mr Rue. Highly appreciate your answer.

Maybe one more question: when I use the bgev distribution and have a look at the hyperparameters via the summary function I get estimates for the spread and the tail and \beta1 for the spread and \beta2 for the tail. Am I right to assume that spread=s_\beta,  tail=\xi ? And what is \beta1 and \beta2? Moreover in the inla.doc("bgev") they set the alpha quantile equal to the linear predictor. Why is this the case?

On Tuesday, 13 June 2023 at 22:09:33 UTC+2 Helpdesk (Haavard Rue) wrote:
> it would be easier to compute quantiles, as you can just pass them
> through...
>
> for the BGEV the expected values has less meaning, and I would suggest
> using a quantile instead (see the original bgev-paper for that)
>
> If you really want the exected value, then you can compute it two ways,
>
> for example, let z=exp(x), we have have density for x and want the
> expected value for z.
>
> 1. compute the density for z, using inla.tmarginal, then compute the
> expected value for 'z' using inla.emarginal, or inla.zmarginal
>
> 2. compute the expected value of exp(x) (wrt to the density of x), using
> inla.emarginal.
>
> approach 2 is more stable.
>
>
>
>

messages.subject: Differential Time Trend - Type II Interaction
messages.subject_clean: Differential Time Trend - Type II Interaction
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am assisting a colleague with their data analysis, specifically using a space-time interaction model. While working on this project, we encountered an issue with the estimates for the TYPE II interaction. We have noticed that these estimates change every time we re-run the same analysis. To illustrate this, I have attached two figures that display histograms of the values obtained from the same model run on two different occasions. The formula and models are below:

###formula
f1a <- age0_5 ~
  f(ID, model = "bym2",graph = g, scale.model = TRUE) +
  f(time, model = "iid") +
  f(Yr_id, model = "rw2") +
  f(ID.area.int <http://ID.area.int>,model="iid", group=ID.year.int <http://ID.year.int>,control.group=list(model="rw2")) # Type II Space-time interaction model - no spatial dependency but with temporal dependency

model1a <- inla(f1a, family="gaussian", data=DF_5,
                inla.mode='experimental',
                control.predictor=list(compute=T),
                control.inla=list(strategy="adaptive", int.strategy="eb",reordering="amdc"),
                control.compute=list(openmp.strategy="huge", smtp="default", dic=TRUE, waic=TRUE),
                verbose=TRUE)
summary(model1a) #157
model1a$ok
########################################

Additionally, I have observed that the verbose output (also attached) contains several recurring errors. Specifically, we encounter the following error message:

*** PARDISO ERROR(0): not pos.def matrix: 1 eigenvalues are negative.
*** PARDISO ERROR: I will try to work around the problem...

It is worth noting that even when we attempt the analysis without using PARDISO, we still encounter a similar error.

Function: GMRFLib_factorise_sparse_matrix_TAUCS(), Line: 740, Thread: 5
Failed to factorize Q. I will try to fix it...

We would greatly appreciate your help in diagnosing and resolving this problem. He has consented to sharing the data with the INLA team, if this would help fix the problem.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Differential Time Trend - Type II Interaction
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Differential Time Trend - Type II Interaction
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The precision matrix from the term
  f(ID.area.int <http://ID.area.int>, model="iid", group = ID.year.int <http://ID.year.int>,
control.group=list(model="rw2"))
is _q I (x) R_, where I is the identity matrix with dimension equals
the number of max(ID.area.int <http://ID.area.int>) = n and R is the precision structure
matrix for the second order random walk which has dimension equals
max(ID.year.int <http://ID.year.int>) = k. Therefore the rank deficiency of this matrix is
2n. Since R has two eigenvalues equals zero, one related to an
eigenvector which is a constant and another which is proportional to a
linear function of 1:k. Because you have  f(Yr_id, model = "rw2") in
the linear predictor, you need to add constraints in order to make the
model proper.

You can add it manually and use model = 'generic0' supplying the
constraints in the extraconstr argument. But a much easier and error
prune option is to exchange the definition by doing
  f(ID.year.int <http://ID.year.int>,control, model="rw1", group=ID.area.int <http://ID.area.int>,
control.group=list(model="iid"))
where the needed constraints are already set.

best regards,
Elias

> > numbers of zeros and ones in my dataset.

> > When using the following code, below, I found the results to be
> > opposite to what I expected. My dataset has approximately 20,000 zeros
> > and 5,000 ones, but my simulations were producing close to 20,000 ones
> > and 5,000 zeros.
> >
> > Is there something wrong with my simulation code for "mu", or how I

> >
> >
> >
> > Nsim=1000
> >
> > Sim <- inla.posterior.sample(n = Nsim, result = Top_model_config)
> > numrows <- nrow(Sim[[1]]$latent)
> >
> > BetaNum <- rownum1
> > #Determines rows for each fixed effect
> > SpatialNum <- rownum3
> > #Determines rows for each mesh node
> > Day <- rownum7
> > #Determines rows for each day
> >
> > N <- nrow(data.df)
> > X <- data.frame(Intercept = rep(1, N),
> >                 VarA = data.df$VarA,
> >                VarB = data.df$VarB,
> >                 VarC = data.df$VarC,
> >                 VarD = data.df$VarD,
> >                 VarE = data.df$VarE)
> >
> > Xm <- as.matrix(X)
> >
> > spatial_sim <- matrix(nrow=N, ncol=Nsim) #Create a matrix to hold our
> > 1000 model realizations, one in each column
> > Zeros <- vector(length = Nsim)
> > #Create 1000 sets of simulated responses from the model realizations
> > mu.i <- matrix(nrow = N, ncol = Nsim)
> > Am   <- as.matrix(A_point)

> >   Betas     <- Sim[[i]]$latent[as.numeric(BetaNum)]

> >  mu.i[,i]  <- exp(FixedPart)/( 1 + exp(FixedPart))
> >   spatial_sim[,i] <- rbinom(n = N, size = 1, prob = mu.i)
> >   Zeros[i] <- sum(spatial_sim[,i] ==0)

messages.subject: varying coefficient models
messages.subject_clean: varying coefficient models
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I would like to fit the following spatial varying coefficient model using  inla package.

y_ij  ~ a_i + b_i * X1_ij + c_i * X2_ij
where y_ij is the response variable for the individual j in the area i. The predictors X1_ij
is a continuous variable and  X2_ij  is a  variable with three categories for the individual j in the area i, respectively.
 when using the following code, below, I'm confused about the meaning of the values obtained through f(). What do the values of area, area1, and area2 represent? If area corresponds to b_i and area1 corresponds to c_i, why does the three-category variable X2_ij have only one value? I might be misunderstanding something. Can you please help clarify?

form<-y_ij ~ 1+
  f(area, X1_ij,
    model = "besag",
    graph =A,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    hyper=list(theta=list(prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.05))), constr =F)+
  f(area1,factor(X2_ij),
    model = "besag",
    graph = A,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    hyper=list(theta=list(prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.05))), constr =F)+
f(area2, model="iid",
    hyper=list(theta=list(prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.05))))
result.form<-
  inla(form,family="gaussian",data=final,verbose = F,
       control.compute = list(dic=TRUE,waic=T,cpo=TRUE,config=TRUE),
       control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
       control.inla=list(strategy='auto', int.strategy='eb'))

result.form[["summary.random"]][["area"]]$'0.5quant'
result.form[["summary.random"]][["area1"]]$'0.5quant'
result.form[["summary.random"]][["area2"]]$'0.5quant'

> categories for the individual j in the area i, respectively.
>  when using the following code, below, I'm confused about the meaning
> of the values obtained through f(). What do the values of area, area1,
> and area2 represent? If area corresponds to b_i and area1 corresponds
> to c_i, why does the three-category variable X2_ij have only one
> value? I might be misunderstanding something. Can you please help
> clarify?
>

>   f(area, X1_ij,
>     model = "besag",
>     graph =A,
>     scale.model = TRUE,
>     hyper=list(theta=list(prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.05))), constr
> =F)+

This term seems find as X1_ij is continous, and constr=F is required as
this is a varying regression coof.

>   f(area1,factor(X2_ij),
>     model = "besag",
>     graph = A,
>     scale.model = TRUE,
>     hyper=list(theta=list(prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.05))), constr
> =F)+

this one I do not understand, as X2_ij is (converted to) a  factor.
wouldn't you rather have a replicated f(area1) for each of the factor
levels??

like this

X2_ij_1 = as.numeric(as.factor(X2_ij) == 1) ## assuming level is 1
X2_ij_2 = as.numeric(as.factor(X2_ij) == 2) ## assuming level is 2

the 'as.numeric' will convert to 0 or 1.

area11 = area1
area12 = area1
n = sizeof graph

f(area11, X2_ij_1, model="besag", scale.model=TRUE,
	hyper = ..., constr=F,
	nrep=2, replicate=rep(1, n)) +
f(area12, X2_ij_2, copy="area11", replicate = rep(2,n))

as you see, you'll get a confounding effect here with the intercept, so
you might set '-1' instead of '1' for the intercept, to get all the
factor levels in.

I think this is the answer to the missing level question of yours.
